stories.headline: COP31: India presses historical responsibility as finance fight drags
stories.summary: At COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, India used the summit's final week to re-centre historical responsibility and equity, arguing that developing countries should not be made to bear the consequences of emissions they did not cause. New Delhi pressed for a two-tier, country-driven Just Transition Mechanism and joined other developing countries in demanding that promised climate finance actually materialise. Ministerial discussions urged Türkiye and Australia to advance fossil fuel transition roadmaps, with Denmark and Spain unveiling fresh plans, even as divisions over energy policy, equity and financing persisted. Opinion writers warned that the summit risks handing the next generation a climate bill, and that declarations continue to outrun the speed, resources and cooperation needed to turn them into practice. Parallel discussions highlighted India's domestic resource-mobilisation challenge and the fragility of high mountain ranges, whose proposed agenda item was reportedly not taken up.
stories.whyItMatters: The summit directly tests the CBDR-RC principle and the credibility of the Paris Agreement's finance architecture — core GS-III environment and GS-II global governance themes for both Prelims and Mains.

perspectives.take: Frames COP31 as India reasserting historical responsibility and pushing a two-tier, country-driven Just Transition Mechanism, while ministers press Türkiye and Australia on fossil fuel roadmaps; Global South-leaning development journalism.

static.topic: Climate Change Regime & India's Commitments
static.syllabusNode: Environment — Climate Change
static.whatIsIt: The UNFCCC (1992) is the parent treaty of the climate regime; the Kyoto Protocol (1997) and the Paris Agreement (2015) operationalise it. India's commitments include net-zero by 2070 and 50% installed non-fossil capacity by 2030.
static.background: The UNFCCC was adopted at the 1992 Rio Earth Summit and entered into force in 1994. Kyoto (1997) placed binding targets on Annex-I parties only; the Paris Agreement (2015) moved to universal, nationally determined contributions with a five-year ratchet and a Global Stocktake. The Loss and Damage Fund was operationalised at COP28 (2023). India leads the International Solar Alliance (2015) and the LiFE mission.
static.geography: Global regime; India's exposure runs from the Himalayan cryosphere to the Indo-Gangetic plains and a long coastline, making adaptation finance a core national interest.
static.socioEconomic: Just transition concerns coal-dependent districts and informal workers; climate finance gaps constrain adaptation spending in developing economies.
static.whyInNews: At COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, India invoked historical responsibility and CBDR-RC and sought a two-tier, country-driven Just Transition Mechanism.
static.wayForward: Operationalise the just-transition mechanism through country-driven plans, close the adaptation finance gap, and link domestic resource mobilisation to NDC implementation.

static.topic: Climate Finance & Just Transition
static.syllabusNode: Environment — Climate Finance and International Cooperation
static.whatIsIt: Climate finance refers to flows from developed to developing countries under the UNFCCC to support mitigation and adaptation. Just transition means ensuring workers and communities dependent on fossil fuels are not left behind.
static.background: The Copenhagen Accord (2009) set a USD 100 billion a year goal for 2020; the Paris Agreement (Article 9) made finance a treaty obligation. The Loss and Damage Fund was operationalised at COP28 (2023), and COP29 (Baku, 2024) agreed a New Collective Quantified Goal of at least USD 300 billion a year by 2035, with calls to scale up to USD 1.3 trillion a year.
static.socioEconomic: Coal-district livelihoods, informal-sector workers and state fiscal capacity shape India's transition pathway; domestic resource mobilisation is central to financing it.
static.whyInNews: India sought a two-tier, country-driven Just Transition Mechanism at COP31, while developing countries demanded delivery on promised finance.
static.wayForward: Blend public, private and multilateral sources; use green bonds and carbon markets; sequence transition plans with worker reskilling and district-level economic diversification.

stories.headline: Xi, Trump and Putin Meet in Historic Trilateral Summit in China
stories.summary: Presidents Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin exchanged greetings in China on 18 November, a day before a trilateral summit on 19 November that participants and much of the world press have labelled historic. The agenda remained unclear even on the eve of the meeting, with reporting noting fears that the three leaders could move towards a carve-up of the world into new 'spheres of influence'. Trump framed the encounter as already a 'win' before it began, while Indian strategic commentary read it as evidence of a new geometry of global power. Coverage also dwelt on the atmospherics of Trump's Asia tour — a handshake with Putin and informal moments — set against high-stakes diplomacy. No joint outcome document or agreed agenda had been publicly confirmed at the time of reporting.
stories.whyItMatters: Directly relevant to GS-II International Relations: great-power competition, multilateralism under strain, and the narrowing space India must navigate between the US, Russia and China. It also feeds ongoing debates on UNSC reform and the future of a rules-based order.

stories.headline: LeT commander Lateef Bhat killed in Kulgam; officer rescued 25 girls
stories.summary: Security forces killed Lashkar-e-Taiba commander Lateef Bhat in an encounter in Kulgam district of south Kashmir, with reports dated 18 November 2026. ThePrint's reconstruction says the manhunt was built on technical and physical surveillance — a dropped mobile phone and a CCTV trail — that allowed forces to fix the commander's location. Telegraph India reports that during the operation an Army officer moved through heavy fire to evacuate 25 girls and two teachers before the commander was neutralised. The Tribune carries the straight news confirmation of the killing, identifying the slain militant as a LeT commander. Together the accounts point to an intelligence-led operation in which civilian evacuation and force protection were run alongside the assault.
stories.whyItMatters: Encounter-based counter-terrorism in Jammu & Kashmir is a recurring GS-III internal security theme, and this case illustrates the shift to technology-driven intelligence and the legal-humanitarian obligation to shield civilians during operations.

static.topic: Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) and India's banned-organisation regime
static.syllabusNode: Internal Security — Terrorism, banned organisations and counter-terror legal framework
static.whatIsIt: LeT is a Pakistan-based militant outfit that has been among the most active groups in Jammu & Kashmir. It operates alongside its charitable front, Jamaat-ud-Dawa, and is listed as a terrorist organisation under Indian law and under the UN Security Council's 1267 sanctions regime.
static.background: LeT was founded in 1990 by Hafiz Muhammad Saeed and is headquartered at Muridke near Lahore, with Markaz-ud-Dawa-wal-Irshad as its parent organisation. India banned it in 2001; the United States designated it a Foreign Terrorist Organisation the same year, and it was listed under the UNSC 1267 sanctions regime in 2005. Its commanders have repeatedly been targeted in encounters in south Kashmir.
static.geography: Headquarters at Muridke, Punjab province, Pakistan; operational footprint in Jammu & Kashmir, particularly the south Kashmir districts of Kulgam, Pulwama, Shopian and Anantnag.
static.socioEconomic: Recruitment has drawn on radical madrasa networks and cross-border infiltration; local recruitment in the Valley has declined in recent years but radicalisation of youth and funding through front charities remain concerns.
static.whyInNews: LeT commander Lateef Bhat was killed in an encounter in Kulgam district, as reported on 18 November 2026.
static.wayForward: Sustain intelligence-led operations against the command structure, choke financing and front-organisation networks, strengthen deradicalisation and rehabilitation programmes, and pursue multilateral sanctions listings against LeT-linked individuals.
prelimsPointers: LeT was founded in 1990 by Hafiz Muhammad Saeed and is headquartered at Muridke near Lahore.
It is banned in India, designated an FTO by the United States, and listed under the UNSC 1267 sanctions regime.

static.mainsAngle: Discuss how India's legal and multilateral instruments against banned organisations complement on-ground counter-terror operations in Jammu & Kashmir.

static.topic: Counter-insurgency architecture in Jammu & Kashmir
static.syllabusNode: Internal Security — Role of security forces, coordination and civil protection in counter-insurgency
static.whatIsIt: Counter-insurgency in Jammu & Kashmir rests on a coordinated grid of the Army, Central Armed Police Forces, the Jammu & Kashmir Police and its specialised units, working under a unified command-and-control structure with intelligence inputs from multiple agencies.
static.background: The framework evolved through the 1990s militancy peak, with the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act of 1958 and its Jammu & Kashmir counterpart of 1990 providing the legal cover for operations in notified 'disturbed areas'. Over time the emphasis shifted from large cordon-and-search operations to small, intelligence-led, targeted strikes on militant leadership.
static.geography: South Kashmir — Kulgam, Pulwama, Shopian and Anantnag — has been the principal theatre of recent leadership-targeting operations; the region's terrain and dense habitation complicate operations.
static.socioEconomic: Prolonged conflict has affected schooling, tourism and livelihoods; operations near schools and habitations raise the risk of civilian casualties and local alienation.
static.whyInNews: The Kulgam operation in which an Army officer evacuated 25 girls and two teachers under fire before the LeT commander was killed.
static.wayForward: Institutionalise civilian-evacuation protocols in encounter sites, invest in technology-enabled surveillance, publish credible post-operation accounts to counter misinformation, and pair kinetic action with development and deradicalisation outreach.
prelimsPointers: The Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act dates to 1958; Jammu & Kashmir has its own version enacted in 1990.
The Jammu & Kashmir Police's Special Operations Group is a dedicated counter-militancy unit.
Operations are coordinated through a unified command structure involving the Army, CAPFs and state police.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate whether intelligence-led targeted operations have improved security outcomes in Jammu & Kashmir, and examine the safeguards needed to protect civilians during such operations.

stories.headline: Gaza ceasefire strains as Trump's Board of Peace faults Israel and Hamas
stories.summary: The Board of Peace set up by President Donald Trump to steer the Gaza agreement has publicly warned that the fragile ceasefire could collapse unless Israel and Hamas recommit to the pledges made during negotiations. Major fighting has been halted, but the wider plan — Hamas disarmament, Israeli troop withdrawal and reconstruction — has effectively stalled since soon after the truce came into force. The warning coincided with a rare Israeli ground operation inside Gaza beyond the 'Yellow Line', which Israel described as the dismantling of a 'terror tunnel' and Hamas condemned as a flagrant ceasefire violation. Reporting also turns to the money question, asking what has become of the roughly $18bn pledged to the Board of Peace for Gaza.
stories.whyItMatters: Gaza is the sharpest live test of whether an externally convened, non-UN framework can hold a ceasefire and deliver reconstruction — directly relevant to GS-II questions on multilateralism, the UN system and West Asian stability, and to India's energy, diaspora and diplomatic stakes in the region.

static.whatIsIt: India recognised Israel in 1950 and established full diplomatic relations in 1992; ties have since expanded in defence, agriculture, water and technology. In parallel, India maintains relations with Palestine and supports a negotiated two-state solution.
static.background: India's traditional support for the Palestinian cause predates 1992; in recent years New Delhi has pursued de-hyphenated ties with Israel and Palestine, and joined the I2U2 grouping with Israel, the UAE and the United States. Instability in the Levant directly touches India's energy imports, its large diaspora in the Gulf and its remittance flows.

static.wayForward: Continue principled support for a two-state solution and unimpeded humanitarian access, protect diaspora and energy interests, and engage all regional stakeholders without abandoning strategic autonomy.

static.topic: International Humanitarian Law and Protection of Civilians
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — International Law / IHL and armed conflict
static.whatIsIt: IHL, the law of armed conflict, governs conduct during hostilities through the Geneva Conventions of 1949 and their Additional Protocols, resting on the principles of distinction, proportionality, precaution and humanity.
static.background: Four Geneva Conventions (1949) and three Additional Protocols (1977 and 2005) form the core; the International Criminal Court was established by the Rome Statute (adopted 1998, in force 2002). The UN Security Council has repeatedly adopted resolutions on the protection of civilians in armed conflict.
static.whyInNews: Alleged violations amid the erosion of the Gaza ceasefire — tunnel operations, military incursions and constrained humanitarian access — sharpen questions of IHL compliance and accountability.
static.wayForward: Independent and verifiable monitoring, guaranteed humanitarian corridors and access, and consistent application of accountability mechanisms to all parties.
prelimsPointers: Four Geneva Conventions (1949) plus three Additional Protocols (1977 and 2005) constitute the core of IHL.
The International Criminal Court sits at The Hague; the Rome Statute was adopted in 1998 and entered into force in 2002.

static.topic: India's air pollution governance framework
static.syllabusNode: Environment — Pollution & Environmental Governance
static.whatIsIt: A layered regime combining the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981 and the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, the Central Pollution Control Board, the National Clean Air Programme (NCAP), the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) and the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) for the NCR and adjoining areas.
static.background: The Air Act, 1981 created pollution control boards; the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 followed the Bhopal gas tragedy and enables umbrella rule-making. GRAP was introduced in 2017 on Supreme Court direction to link graded restrictions to AQI levels. NCAP was launched in 2019 with a target of reducing PM2.5 and PM10 concentrations, later revised to a 40% reduction by 2025-26 across 131 non-attainment cities. The CAQM, first created by ordinance in 2020 and given statutory backing by an Act in 2021, took over coordination for the NCR and adjoining areas.
static.geography: The Indo-Gangetic Plain's landlocked geography, winter temperature inversion, low wind speeds and Himalayan trapping of pollutants concentrate emissions over the NCR; stubble burning in neighbouring states adds to the load.
static.socioEconomic: Air pollution imposes a large health and productivity burden, disproportionately affecting outdoor and informal workers, while crop-residue burning reflects the economics of short sowing windows and limited residue-management alternatives.
static.whyInNews: Delhi's winter air quality crisis has renewed commentary on year-round action, citizen accountability and aligning pollution expenditure with health risk.
static.wayForward: Shift from episodic emergency response to year-round source apportionment and mitigation, strengthen inter-state and regional coordination, expand monitoring networks, and integrate clean fuel, public transport and waste-management measures.
prelimsPointers: GRAP operates in four stages keyed to AQI bands — Stage I (Poor, 201–300), Stage II (Very Poor, 301–400), Stage III (Severe, 401–450) and Stage IV (Severe+, above 450).
NCAP (2019) initially targeted a 20–30% reduction in PM2.5 and PM10 by 2024 with 2017 as base year, later revised to 40% by 2025-26 for 131 non-attainment cities.
CAQM is a statutory body for the National Capital Region and adjoining areas, created by ordinance in 2020 and enacted in 2021.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate whether India's air pollution governance is structured around episodic crisis management rather than sustained, health-risk-based intervention.

static.topic: Health financing and risk-based welfare allocation

static.background: Rights-based laws such as MGNREGA (2005), the RTE Act (2009) and the National Food Security Act (2013) established entitlements, while Ayushman Bharat (2018) extended health coverage and POSHAN Abhiyaan targeted malnutrition. The COVID-19 pandemic exposed gaps in health infrastructure and in how health spending is prioritised.
static.socioEconomic: Allocation choices determine whether expenditure reaches the populations facing the greatest health risk, including those exposed to high ambient air pollution; exclusion errors and urban poverty shape outcomes.
static.whyInNews: The Hindu's opinion argues that COVID-19 lessons on risk-based health spending should inform the response to air pollution.
static.wayForward: Anchor health and pollution budgets to disease burden and exposure data, strengthen primary health infrastructure, and build environmental health surveillance into existing welfare delivery systems.

static.mainsAngle: Should health and environmental expenditure in India be reoriented from input-based outlays to risk- and burden-based allocation? Discuss.

static.topic: Parliamentary oversight and public accountability

static.whatIsIt: Parliament (Article 79) comprises the President, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha; a Bill becomes law after passage by both Houses and Presidential assent (Article 111). Oversight tools include Question Hour, Zero Hour and Departmentally Related Standing Committees.
static.background: Money Bills (Article 110) originate only in the Lok Sabha, where the Rajya Sabha may delay but not amend the money provisions. Ordinances (Article 123) may be promulgated when Parliament is not in session and must be approved within six weeks of reassembly. Departmentally Related Standing Committees scrutinise Bills referred to them.
static.whyInNews: The accountability framing in the air pollution debate raises questions about how consistently legislatures scrutinise environmental and public health measures.
static.wayForward: Strengthen committee referral of environmental and health legislation, ensure regular review of programme outcomes, and publish implementation data to enable citizen accountability.
prelimsPointers: A no-confidence motion can be moved only in the Lok Sabha.
A Bill pending in the Rajya Sabha lapses on dissolution of the Lok Sabha only if it has not yet been passed by the Lok Sabha.
Adjournment, prorogation and dissolution differ in their effect on pending Bills.
static.mainsAngle: Assess declining legislative scrutiny and committee referrals as a governance concern, using environmental regulation as an illustration.

stories.headline: Iran strikes US air base in Kuwait, widening attacks across the Gulf
stories.summary: Iran said it struck a US air base in Kuwait, extending a series of attacks on American facilities in the Gulf that also hit sites in Bahrain on November 13 and November 15. Tehran described the strikes as retaliation for US drone surveillance operations and an attack on Iranian communications towers, while Washington characterised its own earlier actions as defensive strikes. The escalation drew public criticism from Gulf states, which host the very US bases now in the firing line. The widening geography of the exchanges — from Bahrain to Kuwait — signals that the confrontation is no longer confined to a single theatre.

static.whatIsIt: The UN Charter (1945) prohibits the threat or use of force in international relations (Article 2(4)) except in self-defence (Article 51) or when authorised by the UN Security Council under Chapter VII. The 15-member UNSC — five permanent veto-wielding members and ten elected members — holds primary responsibility for international peace and security.
static.background: The UN was founded in 1945 with six principal organs. India is a founding member and among the largest troop contributors to UN peacekeeping. The G4 (India, Brazil, Germany, Japan) campaigns for permanent UNSC seats, while the Intergovernmental Negotiations (IGN) on Security Council reform remain inconclusive.

static.topic: West Asia Security Architecture and India's Gulf Stakes
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and West Asia; Energy Security
static.whatIsIt: West Asia hosts a dense network of US military facilities and a Gulf security order anchored in the GCC states. Any escalation involving Iran, the US and Gulf host nations directly affects shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, global energy prices and the large Indian diaspora in the region.
static.background: The US maintains a substantial military presence in the Gulf, including naval forces headquartered in Bahrain and air and army facilities in Kuwait and Qatar. India's ties with both Iran and the Gulf states rest on energy imports, remittances and trade, and New Delhi has historically urged de-escalation and freedom of navigation.

static.socioEconomic: Millions of Indian workers in the Gulf send home substantial remittances, and Gulf states are major suppliers of India's crude oil and LPG, so conflict-driven price spikes feed into India's inflation and current-account position.
static.whyInNews: Iran struck a US air base in Kuwait and US facilities in Bahrain (November 13 and 15), widening the Gulf conflict and drawing public criticism from Gulf states.
static.wayForward: India should keep diplomatic channels open with both Tehran and the Gulf capitals, maintain contingency plans for evacuation of nationals, and diversify crude sourcing to cushion supply shocks.

stories.headline: India needs a comprehensive doctrine on space security
stories.summary: An opinion piece in The Hindu argues that India lacks a coherent, publicly articulated doctrine for space security even as satellites become central to communication, navigation, surveillance and strategic warning. The author's core argument is that India's aim should not be to turn outer space into another arena of conflict, but to ensure that disruption in orbit — jamming, debris, cyber intrusion or an attack on a satellite — does not translate into vulnerability on Earth. This is set against rising contestation among major powers, the rapid growth of commercial and private space activity, and the steady accumulation of space debris. India's present architecture — ISRO's civilian programme, IN-SPACe and NSIL for private participation, and defence structures such as the Defence Space Agency — is presented as fragmented rather than doctrinal. The piece calls for a comprehensive framework covering deterrence, resilience, attribution and norms-building within the Outer Space Treaty and UN COPUOS framework.
stories.whyItMatters: Space is a cross-cutting UPSC theme spanning GS-III science and technology, internal and external security, and GS-II international governance, and questions on space security, debris and India's space reforms recur regularly.

perspectives.take: Frames space security as a doctrinal gap rather than a hardware gap: India should seek to prevent disruption in space from becoming vulnerability on Earth, not to militarise orbit — a restraint-oriented, norms-plus-resilience framing typical of the paper's strategic commentary.

static.topic: India's Space Programme (ISRO)
static.syllabusNode: Science & Technology — Space
static.whatIsIt: ISRO, established in 1969 under the Department of Space, runs India's civilian space programme across communication, remote sensing, navigation (NavIC) and exploration. Following the 2020 reforms, IN-SPACe promotes and regulates private participation while NSIL serves as the commercial arm.
static.background: Aryabhata (1975) was India's first satellite. The programme expanded through the SLV, PSLV and GSLV launcher families and the INSAT and IRS series. Mangalyaan reached Mars orbit on its first attempt in 2013, Chandrayaan-3 soft-landed near the lunar south pole in 2023, and Aditya-L1 was launched in 2023. Gaganyaan is India's first planned crewed mission.
static.socioEconomic: Space applications underpin telecommunications, broadcasting, weather forecasting, disaster management, agricultural and fisheries advisories, and a fast-growing private space-startup economy.
static.whyInNews: An opinion piece argues that India needs a comprehensive space security doctrine to sit alongside the civilian and commercial expansion of the programme.
static.wayForward: Pair the civilian and commercial push with a declared space security posture covering resilience, attribution, debris mitigation and active norms-building.

India is a founder of the Outer Space Treaty framework; UN COPUOS governs space law.

static.topic: Space Security and India's Institutional Framework

static.whatIsIt: Space security concerns the protection of satellites and their ground segments from jamming, spoofing, cyber intrusion, debris and kinetic attack, together with the norms governing military activity in orbit.
static.background: The Outer Space Treaty (1967) bars placing weapons of mass destruction in orbit and reserves space for peaceful purposes; UN COPUOS is the principal law-making forum, while PAROS discussions at the UN address the prevention of an arms race in outer space. India conducted Mission Shakti, an anti-satellite test, in March 2019, and the Defence Space Agency was set up the same year. The Indian Space Policy 2023 laid out roles for ISRO, IN-SPACe, NSIL and private players.
static.socioEconomic: Heavy dependence on satellites makes both economies and militaries vulnerable to disruption in orbit, while debris threatens the long-term sustainability of commercial space activity.
static.whyInNews: The opinion piece argues that India's objective should be to stop disruption in space from becoming vulnerability on Earth, rather than to turn space into another arena of conflict.
static.wayForward: Adopt a declared doctrine combining deterrence by resilience, attribution capability, debris mitigation and sustained diplomacy in COPUOS and PAROS.

Mission Shakti (March 2019) was India's anti-satellite test in low Earth orbit.

static.mainsAngle: Examine whether India needs a declared space security doctrine, and outline the elements such a doctrine should contain.

stories.headline: Bangladesh deploys paramilitary as unrest grows over Hasina's return
stories.summary: Bangladesh has deployed paramilitary forces to contain spreading unrest linked to the possible return of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who left the country in August 2024 and has since been in India. Police have recorded dozens of crude bomb blasts and incidents of vehicles being torched across at least 28 districts over the past ten days, with several police personnel and civilians injured, according to local media reports carried by both The Hindu and Reuters. The violence marks a fresh escalation in Bangladesh's post-2024 political turbulence and has prompted a heavier security footprint in the districts affected. The deployment signals that authorities expect the agitation to persist rather than subside in the near term.
stories.whyItMatters: Political volatility in Bangladesh directly affects India's neighbourhood diplomacy, border security, connectivity projects and water-sharing agenda. For UPSC, it links India's Neighbourhood First policy with questions of internal stability in South Asian democracies.

perspectives.take: An Indian-outlet framing that foregrounds the scale of the violence — bomb blasts and arson in at least 28 districts over ten days — and implicitly reads the crisis through its consequences for India, where Hasina has been based since 2024.

static.topic: India–Bangladesh Relations
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and its Neighbourhood
static.whatIsIt: The bilateral relationship between India and Bangladesh spanning political, security, economic, connectivity and water-sharing dimensions; Bangladesh is a key pillar of India's Neighbourhood First and Act East policies.
static.background: India supported Bangladesh's Liberation War and recognised the new state in December 1971. The Indira–Mujib Treaty of Friendship, Cooperation and Peace (1972) framed early ties. The Land Boundary Agreement of 1974 was operationalised in 2015 through the Constitution (100th Amendment) Act, which exchanged enclaves. The Ganga Waters Treaty (1996) governs one shared river while Teesta sharing remains unresolved. Ties have fluctuated with changes of government in Dhaka, most sharply after August 2024.
static.geography: India and Bangladesh share roughly 4,096 km of border — India's longest land border with any neighbour. Bangladesh is almost entirely surrounded by India, with the narrow Siliguri Corridor (Chicken's Neck) as India's strategic link to the North-East; the two share the Ganga–Brahmaputra–Meghna delta.
static.socioEconomic: Bangladesh is among India's largest trading partners in South Asia, and India extends lines of credit and connectivity projects including rail links and the BBIN motor vehicles framework. Migration, river water sharing and border management remain recurring socio-economic issues.
static.whyInNews: Bangladesh deployed paramilitary forces after unrest over former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina's possible return, with crude bomb blasts and vehicle arson reported in at least 28 districts.
static.wayForward: India should maintain channels across Bangladesh's political spectrum, expedite pending water-sharing and connectivity agreements, and insulate development cooperation from short-term political volatility in Dhaka.

static.topic: Bangladesh's Political System and Constitutional Transition
static.syllabusNode: Polity & Governance — Constitutional and Political Developments in South Asia
static.whatIsIt: Bangladesh is a parliamentary republic under its 1972 Constitution, with a largely ceremonial President as head of state and a Prime Minister as head of government; the unicameral Jatiya Sangsad has 350 seats — 300 directly elected and 50 reserved for women.
static.background: The 1972 Constitution followed independence in 1971. A caretaker-government system was introduced by the 13th Amendment in 1996 and abolished by the 15th Amendment in 2011. Sheikh Hasina resigned and left Bangladesh in August 2024 amid mass protests; an interim government led by Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus took charge, and the International Crimes Tribunal has since pursued cases relating to the previous regime.
static.socioEconomic: Youth unemployment, disputes over job quotas, inflation and heavy dependence on remittances and garment exports have driven mass mobilisation and shaped the political economy of the crisis.
static.whyInNews: Unrest over Hasina's possible return has triggered paramilitary deployment and violence across multiple districts.
static.wayForward: Credible and inclusive elections, along with institutional safeguards for dissent and rule of law, are essential for Bangladesh's stability and for predictable relations with its neighbours.

static.topic: SAARC, BIMSTEC and Regional Cooperation in South Asia
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Regional Groupings and India's Neighbourhood
static.whatIsIt: SAARC (1985) is the eight-member South Asian regional body, while BIMSTEC (1997) links seven countries around the Bay of Bengal. India has increasingly prioritised BIMSTEC as SAARC remains largely stalled.
static.background: SAARC was founded in Dhaka in 1985 with its secretariat in Kathmandu; its most recent summit was held in Kathmandu in 2014. BIMSTEC, created by the 1997 Bangkok Declaration, has its secretariat in Dhaka and gained salience as India pushed for alternative regional platforms.
static.geography: Bay of Bengal-centred geography links Bangladesh, India, Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Nepal and Bhutan under BIMSTEC, making Bangladesh central to eastward connectivity.
static.socioEconomic: Regional cooperation covers trade, connectivity, energy, disaster management and the blue economy; political stability in Bangladesh is important for the viability of Bay of Bengal connectivity corridors.
static.whyInNews: Political unrest in Bangladesh can disrupt regional connectivity projects and summit-level cooperation among South Asian and Bay of Bengal states.
static.wayForward: Strengthen BIMSTEC's institutional capacity, complete pending connectivity projects, and keep regional platforms insulated from bilateral political shocks.
prelimsPointers: SAARC: founded in 1985 in Dhaka; secretariat in Kathmandu; eight member states.
BIMSTEC: created by the 1997 Bangkok Declaration; seven members; secretariat in Dhaka.

stories.headline: SC issues contempt notice to advocate over remarks against CJI Surya Kant
stories.summary: The Supreme Court has issued a contempt notice to an advocate over remarks directed at Chief Justice of India Surya Kant. Live Law reported that the remarks were treated as insulting to the CJI, while Supreme Court Observer described them as 'unworthy' and noted that the advocate has been put on notice. The development invokes the Supreme Court's contempt jurisdiction, which is meant to protect the administration of justice and the dignity of the court. The matter also touches on the constitutional balance between judicial independence, institutional respect and free speech. Further proceedings will depend on the advocate's response to the notice.
stories.whyItMatters: It tests the scope of contempt jurisdiction and the balance between judicial dignity and Article 19(1)(a) speech, making it relevant to GS-II polity and recent Supreme Court–Bar dynamics.

static.topic: Supreme Court's Contempt Jurisdiction and Judicial Review
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Judiciary: Supreme Court, High Courts & Judicial Review
static.whatIsIt: The Supreme Court is the apex court and guardian of the Constitution under Article 124; as a court of record under Article 129, it can punish for contempt. Judicial review allows it to test laws and executive action against the Constitution.
static.background: Article 124 establishes the Supreme Court; Article 214 establishes High Courts. The collegium system evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998); Kesavananda Bharati (1973) laid down the basic-structure doctrine; PILs expanded access from the late 1970s. Article 32 and Article 226 provide writ jurisdiction.
static.geography: India; the Supreme Court sits at New Delhi.
static.whyInNews: The Supreme Court issued a contempt notice to an advocate over remarks against CJI Surya Kant on 18 November 2026.
static.wayForward: Contempt should be exercised sparingly and through reasoned orders, while courts, bar bodies and the legislature can develop clearer norms to protect judicial independence without chilling legitimate criticism.
prelimsPointers: Article 129 makes the Supreme Court a court of record and empowers it to punish for contempt.
Article 142 permits the Supreme Court to pass any order necessary for complete justice.
The Contempt of Court Act, 1971 distinguishes civil contempt (wilful disobedience) from criminal contempt (scandalising or obstructing justice).
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether the Supreme Court's contempt jurisdiction needs rebalancing with free speech, and suggest institutional safeguards that preserve both judicial dignity and accountability.

prelims: The Supreme Court is a court of record under Article 129 and can punish for contempt.
Article 124 establishes the Supreme Court; Article 214 establishes High Courts.
Article 32 (SC) and Article 226 (HC) provide writ jurisdiction.
The Contempt of Court Act, 1971 governs civil and criminal contempt in India.
stories.mainsQuestion: Critically examine the use of contempt jurisdiction by the Supreme Court to protect judicial dignity. How can this power be balanced with the freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a)?

stories.headline: Omar Abdullah presses Centre to clarify delay in J&K statehood
stories.summary: Omar Abdullah has publicly pressed the Union government to clarify why statehood has not been restored to Jammu and Kashmir, arguing that the people of the region must not be humiliated by indefinite delay. His remarks revive the political demand that full statehood be returned after the 2019 reorganisation of J&K into a Union Territory. The Hindu’s editorial, written in the wake of a terror attack in Kashmir, links durable peace to restoration of statehood, suggesting that security measures alone cannot address the political vacuum. static.topic: Centre-State relations and the Governor’s role
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Federalism & Devolution
static.whatIsIt: India’s quasi-federal arrangement divides powers through the Seventh Schedule; the Governor acts as the Centre’s constitutional representative in States and Union Territories.
static.background: Sarkaria Commission (1983) and Punchhi Commission (2007) reviewed Centre-State balance; the Governor’s assent under Article 200 and reservation under Article 201 have been recurring flashpoints.
static.geography: Jammu and Kashmir, a Union Territory with a legislature, is directly affected by Centre-UT relations.
static.socioEconomic: Political uncertainty can affect investment, tourism, employment and delivery of welfare in J&K.
static.whyInNews: Omar Abdullah’s demand for clarity on statehood highlights Centre-J&K political and constitutional relations.
static.wayForward: A time-bound political roadmap, transparent constitutional process, and cooperative federalism mechanisms such as consultative councils.
prelimsPointers: Concurrent List: union law prevails on repugnancy unless state law reserved for President’s assent (Art. 254).
Inter-State Council (Art. 263) is a recommendatory dispute-resolution body.
static.mainsAngle: Assess whether the delay in restoring J&K statehood reflects a wider problem in Centre-State and Centre-UT federal practice.

static.topic: Internal security and political stability in J&K
static.syllabusNode: Security — Internal Security
static.whatIsIt: Internal security covers terrorism, insurgency and law-and-order challenges, handled by the MHA, IB, NIA and state or UT police.
static.background: Counter-terror frameworks include the NIA (2008), AFSPA in disturbed areas, and the SAMADHAN doctrine for left-wing extremism; J&K has faced decades of terrorism and militancy.
static.geography: Jammu and Kashmir shares borders with Pakistan and China; terrain and border dynamics shape security.
static.socioEconomic: Prolonged security focus can constrain normal political and economic life; peace is linked to political settlement.
static.whyInNews: The Hindu editorial connects a recent Kashmir terror attack to the absence of statehood and elusive peace.
static.wayForward: Combine security operations with political outreach, accountability, and restoration of democratic institutions.
prelimsPointers: NIA (2008) investigates terror offences under the NIA Act.
AFSPA applies to areas declared disturbed under the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act, 1958.
static.mainsAngle: Examine why security-centric responses in J&K need to be complemented by political and constitutional measures.

static.topic: Jammu and Kashmir statehood and Article 370
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Union and its Territory; Jammu and Kashmir
static.whatIsIt: Jammu and Kashmir was reorganised in 2019 into two Union Territories—J&K with a legislature and Ladakh without a legislature—after revocation of Article 370 and enactment of the J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019.
static.background: Article 370 gave J&K special status; Presidential Orders in 2019 and the Reorganisation Act changed its constitutional position. The Supreme Court upheld the abrogation in 2023. Statehood restoration has been demanded by regional parties.
static.geography: J&K is a Himalayan border UT with strategic significance; Ladakh was separated as a UT without a legislature.
static.socioEconomic: Statehood affects legislative powers, fiscal autonomy, and residents’ political representation.
static.whyInNews: Omar Abdullah’s demand and The Hindu editorial renew the statehood question.
static.wayForward: A clear, time-bound roadmap for statehood and restoration of full democratic institutions, alongside security and development measures.
prelimsPointers: The J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019 bifurcated the erstwhile State into the UTs of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh.
Jammu and Kashmir is a Union Territory with a legislature; Ladakh is a Union Territory without a legislature.

stories.summary: European allies of Ukraine gathered in Berlin to signal continued support, even as the battlefield increasingly extends below ground. In parallel, BBC reporting from an old gas pipeline shows Ukrainian forces fighting Russian troops in tunnel networks, seeking cover from drone surveillance. The two developments underscore how the war is being contested through both high-level diplomacy and unconventional subterranean tactics. The Berlin meeting is framed as a show of solidarity, while the pipeline fighting illustrates tactical adaptation on the front lines.

static.topic: UN Security Council and Multilateral Reform
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance
static.whatIsIt: The UN Security Council is the primary organ for international peace and security, with five permanent veto-wielding members and ten elected members. Reform debates focus on expanding permanent and non-permanent seats.
static.background: The UN was founded in 1945. India is a founding member and a leading troop contributor to UN peacekeeping. The G4—India, Brazil, Germany and Japan—campaigns for permanent UNSC seats. The Intergovernmental Negotiations (IGN) on Security Council reform remain inconclusive.
static.whyInNews: The Ukraine war has renewed scrutiny of UNSC decision-making, especially the P5 veto, while European allies coordinate support outside the Council.
static.wayForward: Revitalise IGN talks, build coalitions around representativeness, and address veto reform and Africa's Ezulwini Consensus.

static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Bilateral, Regional and Global Groupings
static.whatIsIt: The Russia-Ukraine war is a major interstate conflict in Europe, with frontline combat, drone warfare, and extensive international sanctions and military support.
static.background: The conflict escalated with Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. European states and NATO allies have provided military, financial and humanitarian support to Ukraine. The war has shifted to attritional and technological warfare, including drone and underground tactics.
static.geography: Eastern Europe; Black Sea region; frontline areas in eastern and southern Ukraine.
static.socioEconomic: Global energy and food security disruptions, refugee flows, defence spending increases, and sanctions on Russia.

stories.headline: Flat ₹5 MDR fee likely for B2B UPI transactions under new payment framework
stories.summary: A new payment framework under discussion is likely to introduce a flat ₹5 merchant discount rate (MDR) on business-to-business (B2B) UPI transactions, marking a departure from the zero-MDR regime that currently applies to UPI person-to-merchant payments. The proposal is aimed at creating a revenue stream for banks and payment system operators who bear the cost of processing these transactions. In parallel, fintech firms have flagged that incentives promised for UPI and RuPay digital transactions remain unpaid, even as the MDR rollout faces delays. Together, the two developments point to a widening gap between the stated economics of India's digital payments push and the actual cash flows reaching the entities that run it. The debate now centres on whether a flat, low-value fee can sustain the ecosystem without deterring merchants, particularly small businesses, from adopting B2B digital payments.
stories.whyItMatters: MDR is the core revenue question for India's UPI ecosystem, and any move to levy it on B2B transactions tests the balance between affordability for merchants and viability for banks and fintechs. It links directly to GS-III questions on digital economy financing and GS-II questions on the state's role in building and sustaining digital public infrastructure.

perspectives.take: Reports the likely design of the new framework — a flat ₹5 MDR on B2B UPI — framing it as a structural shift in how UPI transactions are priced.

Highlights the industry-side friction: fintechs say promised UPI incentives are unpaid and MDR implementation is being delayed, framing the story around implementation credibility rather than policy design.

static.topic: Digital Public Infrastructure & Data Governance
static.syllabusNode: Governance — e-Governance & Data
static.whatIsIt: India's Digital Public Infrastructure — Aadhaar, UPI and DigiLocker — is a layered, interoperable stack. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs personal data processing.
static.background: Aadhaar (UIDAI, 2009) is the world's largest biometric ID. UPI (NPCI, 2016) processes billions of monthly transactions. The DPDP Act introduces a Data Protection Board and consent-based processing.
static.geography: India-wide; the DPI stack is also being pitched as an exportable model to other developing economies.
static.socioEconomic: UPI has become the primary rail for small-value retail payments, deepening financial inclusion; its pricing model therefore has direct distributional consequences for small merchants.
static.whyInNews: A proposed flat ₹5 MDR on B2B UPI transactions, alongside unpaid UPI incentives flagged by fintechs, raises questions about the financing model of the UPI layer of the DPI stack.
static.wayForward: Any pricing change should be evaluated for its effect on merchant adoption, on the viability of payment system operators, and on the transparency of the incentive disbursal mechanism.
prelimsPointers: NPCI operates UPI, RuPay, IMPS and NACH.
The DPDP Act provides for consent, data-principal rights, and significant data fiduciaries.
static.mainsAngle: Balance innovation with privacy and state surveillance; examine DPI as a global export model — and now, also examine who pays for the DPI rails.

static.topic: Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) and the Economics of Digital Payments
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — Banking & Financial Sector / Digital Payments
static.whatIsIt: MDR is the fee a merchant pays to the acquiring bank or payment service provider for accepting a digital payment; it is the principal revenue source for the entities that process card and UPI transactions.
static.background: UPI was launched by NPCI in 2016. MDR has traditionally been charged on card transactions. Through the Payment and Settlement Systems (Amendment) Act, 2019, Parliament enabled the government to mandate zero MDR on specified digital transactions, and UPI and RuPay debit card transactions were subsequently brought under a zero-MDR regime. To compensate the ecosystem, the government has run incentive schemes for the promotion of digital transactions funded through budget allocations.
static.socioEconomic: Zero MDR kept digital payments cheap for merchants and drove rapid adoption, but left banks and fintechs dependent on government incentives and cross-subsidy; unpaid incentives therefore translate into direct revenue stress for these players.
static.whyInNews: A flat ₹5 MDR is reportedly being considered for B2B UPI transactions under a new payment framework, while fintechs report that UPI incentives remain unpaid and MDR implementation is delayed.
static.wayForward: A tiered or flat low-value MDR for B2B flows, paired with a predictable and time-bound incentive disbursal mechanism, would address viability without taxing small-ticket retail payments.
prelimsPointers: MDR is paid by the merchant, not the customer, to the acquiring bank or payment service provider.
NPCI is the umbrella organisation that operates UPI, RuPay, IMPS and NACH.
The Payment and Settlement Systems (Amendment) Act, 2019 enabled the government to mandate zero MDR on specified digital transactions.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether India's zero-MDR model for retail digital payments is financially sustainable, and evaluate the case for differential pricing of B2B versus person-to-merchant UPI transactions.

prelims: MDR (Merchant Discount Rate) is a fee levied on the merchant by the acquiring bank or payment service provider for accepting digital payments.
NPCI, set up in 2016 as the operator of UPI, also runs RuPay, IMPS and NACH.

stories.mainsQuestion: The push for a flat MDR on B2B UPI transactions, alongside complaints of unpaid incentives to fintechs, exposes the financing fault lines of India's digital payments ecosystem. Examine the case for differential pricing of UPI transactions and suggest a sustainable revenue model that does not undermine merchant adoption.

stories.summary: An investigative series published by Newslaundry, drawing on leaked internal documents, examines the functioning of Deutsche Bank and challenges the official assurance that no bank is too big to fail. TheWire.in has carried a contextual explainer on the series, setting out what the leaked material is and why it matters. Read together, the reports reopen a debate that has run since the 2008 global financial crisis: whether the largest banks remain effectively insulated from failure because governments fear the systemic fallout of letting them collapse. The leaks are presented as evidence that supervisory scrutiny and internal risk controls at large global lenders remain contested ground.
stories.whyItMatters: Directly relevant to GS-III questions on banking regulation, systemic risk and the post-2008 reform architecture, and to prelims facts on G-SIBs, Basel III and India's D-SIB framework.

static.topic: Too Big To Fail (TBTF) and Global Systemically Important Banks (G-SIBs)
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — Banking, financial sector reforms and global financial architecture
static.whatIsIt: The 'too big to fail' problem refers to systemically important banks whose disorderly collapse would threaten the wider financial system, prompting states to rescue them with public money. The Financial Stability Board (FSB), strengthened after the 2008 crisis, publishes an annual list of G-SIBs that face higher capital surcharges and stricter supervision.
static.background: The phrase gained currency during the 2008 global financial crisis, when the US and European governments recapitalised large banks. The G20 tasked the FSB and the Basel Committee with designing a framework; the first G-SIB list was published in 2011 and is updated annually. Deutsche Bank, founded in 1870 and headquartered in Frankfurt, is Germany's largest bank and has featured on the G-SIB list.
static.geography: Global — G-SIB designations are made by the FSB and Basel Committee; Deutsche Bank is headquartered in Frankfurt, Germany.
static.socioEconomic: Bailouts transfer private losses to taxpayers, create moral hazard (risk-taking rewarded, losses socialised), and concentrate credit and political power in a few institutions.
static.whyInNews: An investigative series based on leaked internal documents has renewed scrutiny of Deutsche Bank's practices and of whether large banks remain effectively insulated from failure.
static.wayForward: Fuller implementation of Basel III endgame rules, credible resolution and bail-in regimes, ring-fencing of retail banking, and stronger cross-border supervisory cooperation.
prelimsPointers: The FSB publishes the annual G-SIB list; no Indian bank currently figures on it.
G-SIBs face a capital surcharge (higher loss absorbency) over and above Basel III minimums.
Deutsche Bank, founded in 1870, is Germany's largest bank.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how the 'too big to fail' problem distorts risk-taking, and assess the regulatory tools available to make large banks resolvable without public money.

static.topic: Basel III capital and liquidity standards
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — Banking regulation and capital adequacy
static.whatIsIt: Basel III is the post-2008 global standard on bank capital, leverage and liquidity, issued by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS). It raises the quality and quantity of capital (Common Equity Tier 1), adds a capital conservation buffer, a countercyclical buffer, a leverage ratio, and the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) and Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR).
static.background: Basel I (1988) introduced risk-weighted capital; Basel II (2004) added supervisory review and market discipline; Basel III was agreed in 2010-11 in response to the crisis, with 'endgame' revisions finalised in 2017. India began implementing Basel III in April 2013 and completed the main phase-in by 2019.
static.socioEconomic: Higher capital buffers reduce the probability of bank failure and taxpayer bailouts but can raise the cost of credit; calibration is a trade-off between stability and growth.
static.whyInNews: Leaks around a major global bank revive the question of whether capital and liquidity rules are being applied and enforced in letter and spirit.
static.wayForward: Consistent, full and timely implementation across jurisdictions, avoidance of regulatory rollback, and stronger disclosure to enable market discipline.
prelimsPointers: Basel III norms are issued by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, which works under the Bank for International Settlements (BIS).
LCR requires banks to hold enough high-quality liquid assets to survive a 30-day stress scenario; NSFR addresses longer-term funding stability.
India's Basel III phase-in began in April 2013.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss whether post-crisis capital standards have adequately addressed systemic risk, or whether they have merely shifted risk to less-regulated parts of the financial system.

static.topic: India's Domestic Systemically Important Banks (D-SIBs) and the financial stability architecture
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — Banking sector, RBI regulation and financial stability
static.whatIsIt: RBI's D-SIB framework, introduced in 2014, identifies banks whose failure could disrupt the domestic financial system and requires them to hold additional Common Equity Tier 1 capital. India's stability architecture also includes the Financial Stability and Development Council (FSDC), chaired by the Union Finance Minister, and the RBI's periodic Financial Stability Report.
static.background: RBI issued the D-SIB framework in July 2014, based on the BCBS methodology; SBI was designated in 2015, HDFC Bank was added in 2017 and ICICI Bank in 2019. The FSDC was set up in 2010 to institutionalise the mechanism for maintaining financial stability.
static.geography: India
static.socioEconomic: Systemically important banks dominate deposits and credit; their stability is central to household savings, MSME credit and the payment system.
static.whyInNews: Global leaks around a systemically important bank have renewed debate on the 'too big to fail' doctrine, which is directly relevant to India's own D-SIB framework.
static.wayForward: Periodic review of D-SIB designations, robust resolution and deposit insurance mechanisms, and closer supervision of interconnected non-bank entities.
prelimsPointers: RBI's D-SIB framework came in 2014; SBI, HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank are designated D-SIBs.
The FSDC is chaired by the Union Finance Minister and includes the heads of RBI, SEBI, IRDAI and PFRDA.
DICGC insures bank deposits up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank.
static.mainsAngle: How far does India's D-SIB framework address the 'too big to fail' problem, and what further reforms are needed to protect depositors and taxpayers?

prelims: The Financial Stability Board publishes an annual list of global systemically important banks (G-SIBs); no Indian bank is currently on it.
Basel III standards are framed by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, which functions under the Bank for International Settlements.
RBI's D-SIB framework (2014) requires designated banks to hold additional CET-1 capital; SBI, HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank are designated.
Deutsche Bank, founded in 1870 and headquartered in Frankfurt, is Germany's largest bank.
stories.mainsQuestion: The recurring 'too big to fail' problem suggests that post-2008 financial regulation has not fully resolved the moral hazard created by systemically important banks. Critically examine this in the light of recent leaks concerning a major global bank, and suggest reforms relevant to India.

stories.headline: Bombay High Court sets aside ICICI Bank's sanction to prosecute Chanda Kochhar
stories.summary: The Bombay High Court has set aside the sanction granted by ICICI Bank that formed the basis for prosecuting former bank chief Chanda Kochhar in the ICICI–Videocon loan case. Reports of the 18 November 2026 order describe it as quashing the bank's sanction, which had been treated as a precondition for the prosecution to proceed. The underlying case relates to loans extended by ICICI Bank to the Videocon Group, a matter that has been under investigation for several years. The immediate effect is that the prosecution cannot rest on the sanction as it stood, though the order does not by itself decide the merits of the allegations. The ruling turns on the legality of the sanctioning process rather than on the factual guilt or innocence of the accused.

static.topic: High Courts and judicial review of administrative sanctions

static.whatIsIt: The Bombay High Court, acting as a constitutional court, set aside the sanction granted by ICICI Bank that was to serve as the precondition for prosecuting Chanda Kochhar in the ICICI–Videocon loan case.
static.background: High Courts are constitutional courts under Article 214, and Article 226 gives them writ jurisdiction to quash orders that are illegal, arbitrary or without jurisdiction. The collegium system evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998); Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic-structure doctrine; PILs from the late 1970s widened access to judicial review, while Article 32 (SC) and Article 226 (HC) remain the writ routes.
static.whyInNews: The High Court's order removes the sanction on which the prosecution in the ICICI–Videocon loan case was to proceed against Chanda Kochhar.
static.wayForward: Judicial review of sanctions must balance protection against vexatious prosecution with timely accountability; reasoned and time-bound disposal of such challenges serves both objectives.
prelimsPointers: Article 226 lets High Courts issue writs both for enforcement of fundamental rights and 'for any other purpose' — wider than Article 32.
Article 214 provides a High Court for each state; Article 215 makes it a court of record.

static.topic: Sanction for prosecution under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988
static.syllabusNode: Governance — Transparency and Accountability; statutory safeguards in anti-corruption law
static.whatIsIt: The Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, as amended in 2018, requires prior sanction (Section 19) before a court can take cognisance of specified offences by a public servant, and prior approval (Section 17A) before an inquiry or investigation is conducted.
static.background: The PC Act, 1988 consolidated India's anti-corruption law. The 2018 amendment made changes to the definition of 'public servant', added Section 17A requiring prior approval for inquiry or investigation, and reworked several offence provisions. Courts have repeatedly emphasised that the sanctioning authority must apply its mind to the material placed before it.
static.socioEconomic: In loan-misuse and bank-fraud cases the sanctioning authority is often the bank itself, so the procedure for granting or refusing sanction directly affects how quickly accountability is fixed in the financial sector.
static.whyInNews: The Bombay High Court set aside the sanction granted by ICICI Bank to prosecute Chanda Kochhar, which had been the basis for proceeding in the Videocon loan case.
static.wayForward: Consider statutory timelines and reasoned orders for sanction decisions, and clearer guidance on the competent authority for officials of private-sector banks.
prelimsPointers: The PC Act was enacted in 1988 and substantially amended in 2018.
Sanction under Section 19 is a condition precedent for a court to take cognisance of an offence under the Act.
static.mainsAngle: Sanction for prosecution is defended as a shield against vexatious litigation but criticised as a tool of delay. Examine this tension in the context of economic offences.

stories.headline: Court-driven push for a statutory fix to regulate private universities
stories.summary: Opinion commentary and ongoing litigation have converged on the question of how India regulates private universities and educational campuses. One strand of commentary urges the Ministry of Education to act without delay and issue a statutory notification, consistent with the court's judgment, so that eligible campuses are brought under a clear and enforceable regulatory framework. A parallel strand argues that the deeper problem is opacity: financial information of higher education institutions remains murky, faculty profiles are outdated or absent, regulatory approvals are missing or stale, and employability and dropout rates are rarely disclosed. Meanwhile, the litigation itself has seen procedural movement, with the case on regulating private universities shifted from Justice Amanullah's bench. Together, the developments point to a regulatory architecture that is being pushed towards reform by the judiciary while facing a persistent transparency deficit.
stories.whyItMatters: Higher education regulation sits at the intersection of governance, judicial review and social-sector delivery, and is a recurring GS-II theme on regulatory bodies, accountability and the State's role in education. The transparency gap also feeds directly into debates on student welfare, employability and institutional accountability.

static.topic: Regulation of Higher Education in India
static.syllabusNode: Governance — Government Policies & Interventions; Issues relating to development and management of Social Sector/Services relating to Education
static.whatIsIt: India's higher education sector is regulated by a web of statutory bodies — principally the University Grants Commission (UGC) for general higher education and the All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE) for technical education — alongside professional councils and State university legislation.
static.background: The UGC was set up in 1953 and became statutory under the UGC Act, 1956, with a mandate to coordinate and maintain standards in higher education. AICTE, created in 1945 as an advisory body, was given statutory status in 1987. Education was moved from the State List to the Concurrent List by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment (1976), enabling a larger Union role. The National Education Policy 2020 proposed replacing the multiplicity of regulators with a single Higher Education Commission of India (HECI) with separate verticals for regulation, accreditation, funding and general education.
static.socioEconomic: Private and deemed-to-be universities account for a substantial and growing share of enrolment; uneven standards, fee opacity and weak grievance redressal are recurring concerns for students and parents.
static.whyInNews: Opinion commentary and litigation over how private universities and educational campuses should be regulated, with the Ministry of Education urged to issue a statutory notification consistent with a court judgment.
static.wayForward: Operationalise a single, light-touch but enforceable regulator as envisaged by NEP 2020, with clear entry norms, mandatory public disclosure and a graded sanctions regime.
prelimsPointers: UGC — set up in 1953, made statutory under the UGC Act, 1956.
Education was shifted to the Concurrent List by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment, 1976.
NEP 2020 proposes HECI as a single higher-education regulator with four verticals.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether India's fragmented higher-education regulatory architecture can ensure quality and accountability amid expanding private provision.

static.topic: Judicial Review and the Regulation of Private Universities

static.whatIsIt: Courts exercise writ jurisdiction (Articles 32 and 226) and appellate jurisdiction (Article 136) over regulatory decisions affecting universities, including recognition, affiliation, standards and fees.
static.background: The higher judiciary has repeatedly intervened in higher-education regulation — on deemed university status, admissions to medical and technical courses, and fee regulation — often directing regulators to frame or notify rules. Allocation of cases to particular benches is an administrative function exercised under the authority of the Chief Justice.
static.socioEconomic: Uncertainty over recognition and approvals affects the validity of students' degrees, their employability and the financial viability of institutions.
static.whyInNews: A case concerning the regulation of private universities was shifted from Justice Amanullah's bench, while commentators argue the Ministry must issue a statutory notification consistent with the court's judgment without delay.
static.wayForward: Timely compliance with judicial directions through statutory notifications, alongside clearer listing and roster practices to reduce procedural delay.
prelimsPointers: Article 32 — writ jurisdiction of the Supreme Court; Article 226 — writ jurisdiction of High Courts.
Article 136 — special leave to appeal to the Supreme Court.
Allocation of cases to benches is an administrative function of the Chief Justice, not a judicial determination.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the judiciary's role in shaping regulatory policy in education and the institutional implications of court-mandated regulatory reform.

static.topic: Transparency and Accreditation in Higher Education

static.whatIsIt: Disclosure norms for higher education institutions cover accreditation status, financial statements, faculty details, regulatory approvals, placement and employability outcomes, and dropout rates.
static.background: The National Assessment and Accreditation Council (NAAC) was established in 1994 by the UGC to assess and accredit institutions. The National Institutional Ranking Framework (NIRF) was introduced in 2016 to rank institutions on published parameters covering teaching and resources, research, graduation outcomes, outreach and inclusivity, and perception. Mandatory disclosure requirements exist under UGC regulations, but compliance and comparability across institutions remain uneven.
static.socioEconomic: Students and parents lack reliable information for informed choice, while opacity hampers employer trust and the ability of institutions to be held to account.
static.whyInNews: Commentary argues that financial information of higher education institutions remains murky, faculty profiles are outdated or absent, regulatory approvals are missing or stale, and employability and dropout rates are rarely disclosed.
static.wayForward: Standardised, machine-readable public disclosures; linking accreditation and funding to verified data; independent audit of institutional claims.

NIRF — launched in 2016 to rank higher education institutions on published parameters.

He also linked the setback in the United States midterms to what he described as an erosion of American power. The remarks, delivered on a foreign campus, triggered a sharp political row at home, with the BJP accusing him of peddling "anti-India propaganda" abroad. The episode has revived the recurring debate over the appropriate platform for domestic political criticism and over competing narratives on the health of the Indian economy.

static.topic: Role of the Opposition and Parliamentary Accountability
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Parliament & Legislative Process
static.whatIsIt: Parliament under Article 79 consists of the President, the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha. The Opposition's constitutional function is to scrutinise the executive, extract accountability and offer an alternative policy narrative, both inside and outside the legislature.
static.background: Key mechanisms of accountability include Question Hour, Zero Hour, adjournment motions, no-confidence motions (Lok Sabha only), and Departmentally Related Standing Committees that scrutinise Bills. A Bill becomes law after passage by both Houses and Presidential assent under Article 111; Money Bills (Article 110) originate only in the Lok Sabha, where the Rajya Sabha may delay but not amend the money provisions. Ordinances under Article 123 may be promulgated when Parliament is not in session and must be approved within six weeks of reassembly.
static.socioEconomic: Declining sitting days and falling committee referrals have weakened legislative scrutiny, pushing political contestation increasingly into public and media spaces, including foreign platforms.
static.whyInNews: Rahul Gandhi's remarks at Columbia University, and the BJP's response, spotlight the Opposition's strategy of carrying its critique of the government to international forums.
static.wayForward: Strengthen institutional channels of accountability — more sitting days, mandatory committee referral of Bills, and structured debates — so that substantive policy disagreement is aired within Parliament rather than primarily outside it.
prelimsPointers: A no-confidence motion can be moved only in the Lok Sabha.
A Bill pending in the Rajya Sabha lapses on dissolution of the Lok Sabha only if it has not yet been passed by the Lok Sabha.
Adjournment, prorogation and dissolution differ in their effect on pending Bills.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether the declining use of parliamentary instruments of accountability is shifting political contestation outside Parliament, and assess the implications for representative governance.

static.topic: Manufacturing-led Growth and the Indian Economic Narrative
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Growth, Development & Industrial Policy
static.whatIsIt: Manufacturing-led growth refers to the strategy of expanding the organised industrial base to absorb surplus labour, raise productivity and reduce dependence on services and agriculture for employment.
static.background: The National Manufacturing Policy (2011) set a target of raising manufacturing's share of GDP to 25 per cent. Make in India was launched in September 2014 to boost the sector, and Production Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes were introduced from 2020 across several sectors. Despite these, manufacturing's share in output and employment has remained broadly stagnant, and the sector's contribution to job creation has lagged expectations.
static.geography: Industrial clusters are concentrated in a few states and corridors, contributing to regional divergence in industrial employment.
static.socioEconomic: Weak manufacturing job creation limits the structural transformation of a young workforce, keeping a large share of workers in low-productivity agriculture and informal services.
static.whyInNews: Rahul Gandhi's claim of manufacturing decline in India forms the economic core of the controversy over his Columbia University address.
static.wayForward: Address supply-side constraints — land, logistics, credit access for MSMEs, skill mismatch and regulatory predictability — alongside demand-side measures to raise industrial competitiveness and employment elasticity.
prelimsPointers: Make in India was launched in September 2014.
The National Manufacturing Policy (2011) targeted a 25 per cent share for manufacturing in GDP.
PLI schemes were introduced from 2020 to boost domestic manufacturing across identified sectors.
static.mainsAngle: Critically examine why India's manufacturing share has stagnated despite successive industrial policy interventions, and suggest measures to make manufacturing an engine of employment.

stories.headline: India must deepen Asian partnerships as Japan backs ASEAN strategic autonomy
stories.summary: Two commentaries published the same day converge on one theme: Asia's middle powers are hedging against intensifying US-China rivalry, and India risks losing influence if it treats its Asian relationships as episodic summitry rather than sustained engagement. The Hindu's editorial argues that New Delhi must shore up its partnerships across Asia, from ASEAN to Japan and the wider Indo-Pacific, and give its Act East agenda more institutional depth. ORF's analysis frames Japan as a quiet but effective underwriter of ASEAN's strategic autonomy, using economic assistance, defence cooperation and capacity-building to keep Southeast Asia from being forced to choose sides. Read together, the pieces point to a natural division of labour in which Delhi and Tokyo coordinate to preserve ASEAN centrality and keep the regional order open. The common driver is the shrinking space for non-alignment, which has made multi-alignment, hedging and minilateral groupings the default strategies of Asian states.

static.background: Rooted in NAM (1961) and Panchsheel (1954). Post-1991 liberalisation and the 1998 nuclear tests reshaped ties with the US. The Indo-Pacific concept and Quad (with the US, Japan and Australia) gained salience after 2017.

static.topic: Act East Policy and ASEAN-India Relations
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements involving India; India and its neighbourhood
static.whatIsIt: The Act East Policy is the 2014 successor to the 1991 Look East Policy, prioritising ASEAN and the wider Indo-Pacific through connectivity, trade, defence and cultural ties. ASEAN centrality and the ASEAN Outlook on the Indo-Pacific (AOIP) are its organising principles.
static.background: Look East Policy launched in 1991 under P.V. Narasimha Rao. India became a sectoral dialogue partner of ASEAN in 1992, a full dialogue partner in 1995, and a Summit-level partner in 2002. India joined the East Asia Summit in 2005. The ASEAN-India FTA in goods came into force in 2010, followed by services and investment agreements in 2015. The Act East Policy was announced in 2014 at the East Asia Summit in Nay Pyi Taw. India endorsed the AOIP in 2019 and ties were elevated to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership in 2022.
static.geography: Southeast Asia and the wider Indo-Pacific; ASEAN's ten members span mainland and maritime Southeast Asia, straddling the Strait of Malacca and the South China Sea.
static.socioEconomic: Connectivity projects, trade integration, the Indian diaspora and people-to-people links underpin the economic pillar of Act East; Japan's assistance model in Southeast Asia is often cited as a benchmark for delivery.
static.whyInNews: The editorial on India's Asia diplomacy and ORF's piece on Japan strengthening ASEAN's strategic autonomy both foreground the need to give Act East a sharper Japan-ASEAN dimension.
static.wayForward: Prioritise project delivery and connectivity financing, deepen defence and maritime cooperation with ASEAN states, and coordinate with Japan on capacity building so that ASEAN centrality is preserved rather than eroded.
